11896-citizen-bird-scenes-from-bird-life:
Citizen Bird teaches bird life in plain English for beginners, through conversations between children and adults watching birds in gardens, fields, and woods. Young listeners ask why robins scatter dried huckleberries on snow, why eggs do not freeze. What birds find to eat when everything is frozen stiff.

The answers come as short, vivid scenes rather than lectures, with nests, eggs, songs, and feeding habits described in everyday words. Written for children new to natural history, the book treats birds as neighbors to observe closely. Curiosity, rather than a list of facts, as the way into the subject.
21252-the-practical-distiller-an-introdu:
Samuel McHarry of Lancaster County, Pennsylvania, published The Practical Distiller at Harrisburg in 1809. His aim was whiskey, gin, brandy, and other spirits of better quality and in larger quantity than the common method gave. His raw materials are American: rye, corn, buckwheat, apples, peaches, potatoes, pumpkins, and turnips.

Directions cover every branch of distilling, plus purifying, clearing, and colouring whiskey and imitating French brandy from local spirits. Extracts of approved receipts for cider, domestic wines, and beer close the book. McHarry wrote for a young republic of farmer-distillers, when whiskey was a cash crop in liquid form.
21681-a-little-traitor-to-the-south-a-wa:
Cyrus Townsend Brady mixes comedy and tragedy in A Little Traitor to the South, copyrighted in 1903. Miss Fanny Glen detests a masterful man above all beings on earth. Rhett Sempland, at that moment, looks exactly like such a man to her.

Chapters pit hero against gentleman in a strife of magnanimity. A strong room, an engine of destruction, and the hour and the man raise the stakes. A. D. Rahn draws the pictures and C. E. Hooper the decorations. Brady, a clergyman turned novelist, sets love and honour at war in the Civil War's shadow.
2400-vikram-and-the-vampire-classic-hind:
Richard F. Burton's Vikram and the Vampire retells the classic Hindu tales in which King Vikram must carry a vampire through the night, listening to its stories and answering its riddles. The frame, borrowed from the Sanskrit Vetala tales, gives Burton room for adventure, magic, and moral puzzles, all in his rich, learned English. The stories are earthy, witty, and strange.

Burton, the great Victorian explorer and translator, treats the tales as both entertainment and ethnography. The volume delights readers who love world folklore in its wilder forms. It pairs well with his Arabian Nights.
30499-history-of-free-thought-in-referen:
Adam Storey Farrar delivers eight lectures on the history of free thought in reference to the Christian religion, preached before Oxford University in 1862 on the Bampton foundation. Published in New York in 1863, the volume opens with the will of Rev. John Bampton, canon of Salisbury, plus a preface and analysis.

Lectures move from the subject, method, and purpose of the course to heathen literary opposition in early ages. Later talks cover free thought in the Middle Ages and Renaissance, deism in England before 1760, infidelity in France, and unbelief in England after 1760. Farrar traces dissent with scholarly care, aiming to meet doubt by understanding its history.
35169-encyclopaedia-britannica-11th-edit:
Encyclopaedia Britannica, in this portion of its eleventh edition, covers the alphabetical range from Electrostatics toward Engineering. The text is one stretch of the famous 1911 reference work. Its pages gather hundreds of signed articles, large and small. The transcriber's notes that open the file list corrections made in several of them.

Electrotherapeutics receives the longest run of those corrections. Medical uses of electric current, and the reactions of nerve and muscle, fill that article. Scottish county history enters with the article on Elginshire and its town of Findhorn. Literary biography follows in the life of George Eliot within the same stretch. Her historical novel Romola is weighed in the passage the notes correct. The slice thus shows the eleventh edition's whole method in miniature. Science, place, and letters stand side by side in alphabetical order.
40929-the-transformation-of-early-christ:
Lyford Paterson Edwards wrote a dissertation on early Christianity's change. The University of Chicago granted his doctorate for it. The Collegiate Press issued the book in 1919. Its full title names a shift from end-times faith to social form. Church history was his field of study. Five chapters carry the argument.

Political theories of the first Christians open it. The early church and property concepts follow. The church and the populace take chapter three. Chiliasm and patriotism pair in the fourth. Chiliasm and social theory close the course. Hebrew, Greek, and Roman thought met in the young faith, he opens. Each shaped the church's view of the state, he says. No new political notions came from the faith itself, he claims. A young scholar's thesis traces how a faith awaiting the end learned to build for the long run.
46834-evolution-its-nature-its-evidence-:
Evolution is a treatise by Joseph Le Conte, professor of geology and natural history in the University of California. Appleton of New York printed the second edition, revised, in 1897. Its full title states the program: the nature of evolution, its evidences, and its relation to religious thought. Le Conte also wrote Religion and Science.

The preface to the second edition explains the revision. Three years since the first edition had been years of great activity of thought on his subjects. Among the foremost writers on evolution a warm discussion had sprung up on the factors of evolution, their number and relative importance. Le Conte therefore added a whole chapter on that fight. Later he takes up first and second causes, general and special providence, and mind against mechanics in nature. His book was America's chief attempt to keep Darwin and faith in one house.
48586-the-war-stonewall-jackson-his-camp:
The War is a Confederate memoir by James Wood, a captain in the 37th Virginia Infantry. Its full title joins Stonewall Jackson's campaigns and battles to the story of his regiment. Wood wrote it as he himself saw the events. A portrait of the author in 1910 fronts the book. The Eddy Press of Cumberland, Maryland, published it. He dedicated it to his four children.

The first chapter opens at the Virginia Military Institute. Wood was a cadet there in his teens. He recalls the war spirit rising in 1860 and 1861. Sectional strife in Congress fills his first pages. Lincoln's election deepened fear in the South, he says. Then came secession, state by state, and the fall of Sumter. Regiment memoirs like this one kept local memory alive. Veterans and families were their chief readers.
59227-index-of-the-project-gutenberg-wor:
David Widger made the Index of the Project Gutenberg Works of Charlotte Perkins Gilman. Herland leads the roll of her books in this plain guide. The Yellow Wallpaper, her famed short tale, stands second in line. Each book’s own contents list stands printed in full below.

Our Androcentric Culture walks man made family, art, and law in turn. What Diantha Did and The Crux fill the tale shelf of the set. Concerning Children weighs minding, schooling, and the nurse maid’s part. The Home weighs house work and its grip on women’s lives. Suffrage Songs and Verses adds her fighting rhymes to the roll. Women and Economics, her landmark study, closes the named shelf. The Forerunner, her own monthly, stands in its first volume here. Chapter by chapter, the index lays each volume bare for the reader.
60159-identification-of-the-larger-fungi:
Identification of the Larger Fungi is a field guide by Roy Watling, a principal scientific officer at the Royal Botanic Garden in Edinburgh. Hulton Educational Publications issued it in 1973, in the Hulton Group Keys series. Watling dedicated the book to his parents, who encouraged his interest in mushrooms and toadstools.

The guide teaches method before names. Chapters cover where to look, collecting, examination with the naked eye, and microscopic examination. Then a key to the major groups of larger fungi begins. Agarics and their relatives come first, with keys to the major genera and to the agarics of woodlands and copses. Pored and toothed fungi follow, including the colonisers of tree trunks and stumps and the destroyers of timber in buildings. The key format lets a collector work from specimen to name step by step.
60488-meditations-on-the-essence-of-chri:
Guizot wrote Meditations on the Essence of Christianity, translated from the French under his own supervision and published by John Murray in London in 1864. François Guizot was a French historian and statesman who turned in later life to religious questions. His preface argues that Christianity, often attacked over nineteen centuries, faces a serious new attack in his day.

Eight meditations make up the book. They treat natural problems, Christian dogmas, and the supernatural. Later chapters weigh the limits of science, revelation, and the inspiration of Scripture. The last two present God according to the Bible and Jesus Christ according to the Gospels. Guizot writes as a Protestant layman defending the core of the faith with reason and history, for readers troubled by modern doubt.
65867-philosophical-transactions-vol-l-p:
Part one of volume fifty of the Philosophical Transactions gathers the papers of the Royal Society for the year 1757. It was printed in London in 1758 for the Society's printers, Davis and Reymers. The title promises an account of the undertakings and labours of the ingenious in many parts of the world. The first paper gives an account of an earthquake felt in New England. A paper on the specific gravity of living men follows. A Lisbon surgeon tells of a gut cut through by a knife, and its cure.

A visitation of the leprous persons in the isle of Guadeloupe is reported in a letter. The late finds of antiquities at Herculaneum get their account. The president of the Society, the Earl of Macclesfield, stands over the whole as its head. The volume is science in its club age, told by letter and read paper.
67852-model-aeroplanes-and-their-engines:
George A Cavanagh wrote Model Aeroplanes and Their Engines as a hands-on book for new builders. Moffat, Yard and Company issued it in New York with a nineteen hundred sixteen copyright. Cavanagh edited model news for Aerial Age. Harry G Schultz drew the plans and charts.

Early pages trace the past of model flight. Next come propellers, wings, frames, and launch gear. Floats for water starts get their own steps. Record models from clubs round the world fill one part. Power plants range from wound rubber to pressed air. Small gas and steam plants close the power survey. A word list of flight terms ends the book. Boys who built and flew models in that age found a full shop guide here.
britannica-1911-alamanni-luigi:
Luigi Alamanni, who lived from 1495 to 1556, was an Italian statesman and poet. An entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica follows his exiles and embassies. He was born at Florence, where his father backed the Medici. A felt wrong turned the son against that powerful house.

Alamanni joined a failed plot against Giulio de Medici. Flight to Venice and then to France saved his life. When Florence threw off papal rule in 1527 he came home. Medici return in 1530 drove him back to France for good. French kings trusted him as envoy to great courts. A quick reply of his once won praise from the emperor himself. Most of his verse was written in that French exile. His farm poem in the manner of Virgil ranks as his best.
britannica-1911-anichini-luigi: Ferrara-born Luigi Anichini made his name at Venice around 1550, cutting seals and medals on a tiny scale. Praise for one piece came from Michelangelo himself, who judged Anichini's Interview of Alexander the Great with the high-priest at Jerusalem the art at its most perfect. Collectors also prize his medals showing Henry II of France and Pope Paul III.
britannica-1911-bracket-fungi:
Bracket fungi are hard, woody growths shaped like small half-round shelves on trees and timber, and the entry explains what they are and why they harm woodland. The name comes from their bracket shape. They sit in the order Polyporeae, marked by a layer of tubes or pores on the underside where the spores form.

Inside the tree, the fine root-like part of the fungus spreads through the wood and can kill the host. The visible bracket is only the fruiting stage, yet it sheds huge numbers of spores that enter other trees through wounds or cut surfaces. Many brackets live for years, adding a fresh pore layer each season, which is why the entry stresses care in forestry.
britannica-1911-cibrario-luigi:
Cibrario, Luigi, Count (1802–1870) was an Italian statesman and historian, born in Usseglia on 23 February 1802 to a noble but poor Piedmontese family. He won a scholarship at sixteen and was teaching literature at eighteen, and verses to Prince Charles Albert began a long royal intimacy. He entered the Sardinian civil service and lectured on canon and civil law from 1824. His chief interest was old documents, and he searched Swiss, French and German archives for Savoy charters.

Senator from 1848, he served as finance minister in 1852, then education minister under Cavour, then foreign minister during the Crimean war. He helped win Piedmont admission to the congress of Paris on equal footing with the great powers, and was created count on retiring. His chief work was Economia politica del medio evo in 1839, with a later study of slavery and serfdom. He died in October 1870 near Salò on Lake Garda.
britannica-1911-cornaro-luigi:
Luigi Cornaro (1467-1566) was a Venetian nobleman famed for his writings on a spare, temperate life, as this 1911 Britannica article tells. In his youth he lived freely, but after a grave illness at forty he began, on medical advice, to cut down his diet by degrees. For a time he kept to twelve ounces of solid food and fourteen ounces of wine a day.

Later he cut his fare still further, finding he could live on no more solid food than an egg a day. At eighty-three he wrote his treatise on the sure way to a long and healthful life, and three more on the same theme followed at eighty-six, ninety-one, and ninety-five. The first three came out at Padua in 1558. Addison praised their cheerful, pious good sense, and Cornaro died at Padua at ninety-eight.
britannica-1911-cremona-luigi:
Luigi Cremona (1830-1903) was an Italian mathematician, born at Pavia, as this 1911 Britannica article recounts. At seventeen he joined the Italian volunteers when Milan and Venice rose against Austria, and fought until the fall of Venice in 1849. He then went back to Pavia to study under Francesco Brioschi, aiming at a career teaching mathematics.

Cremona taught first at Cremona and Milan, then held chairs of higher geometry at Bologna and at Milan. In 1866 he shared the Steiner prize of the Berlin Academy for a treatise on surfaces of the third order, and two years later won it alone. In 1873 he was called to Rome to set up the college of engineering. His fame became European, and in 1879 he was made a senator of the kingdom of Italy.
britannica-1911-galvani-luigi:
Luigi Galvani, the man of frog legs, opens a life in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Born at Bologna in 1737, he wished at first for the Church. His parents steered him to a doctor's path at that school. In 1762 he took a public chair to teach body craft there. Skill in teaching and bird body lore soon made his early name.

His fame rests on a claim of animal power in flesh. In 1791 he set out that claim in a famed tract on force. Tales say a frog's leg jerked at a scalpel's touch in 1786. Papers of his school show he chased that spark far earlier. Hooks of copper on iron rails made dead frog legs twitch. That sight drove his search for a power hid in muscle.
britannica-1911-gingi:
Gingi, also called Gingee, a rock fort of southern India, is described in a brief 1911 Britannica article. It lies in the South Arcot district of Madras. Three hills are joined by walls that ring an area of seven square miles. The fort is held to be near proof against attack. Its start is lost in legend.

Held by the Mahrattas at the end of the 1600s, Gingi stood an eight year siege by the armies of Aurangzeb. In 1750 the French took it and held it with a strong force for eleven years. It gave up to the English in 1761. A quote from Orme says that fall ended the long fight between the two powers in Coromandel.
britannica-1911-lanzi-luigi:
Luigi Lanzi, an Italian scholar of old art who lived from 1732 to 1810, is profiled in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. He was educated as a priest. In 1773 he was made keeper of the galleries at Florence. From then on he gave his work to the painting of Italy and to the remains and tongue of the Etruscans.

His history of painting in Italy came out in two parts, in 1792 and in 1796, and Roscoe put it into English. In the study of old remains his great work was an essay on the Etruscan tongue in 1789. He argued that the tongue must be kin to those of the peoples round it, the Romans, Umbrians, Oscans, and Greeks. In a memoir on the painted vases called Etruscan he saw, rightly, that they were Greek in source and style.
britannica-1911-pulci-luigi:
Luigi Pulci, an Italian poet who lived from 1431 to 1487, is the subject of a brief 1911 Britannica article. He was born at Florence, from a well placed family. His elder brother Luca was also a poet, known for three named works. Luigi had the backing of Cosimo, Piero, and Lorenzo de' Medici.

Pulci wrote works in both verse and prose. His fame rests on one long poem, Morgante Maggiore, printed at Venice in 1481. The poem tells of a giant who turns to the Christian faith and travels with Orlando. The piece credits Pulci as the first to bring fine romance into Italian writing.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-adelophagi:
Adelophagi, from Greek words for secretly and I eat, was a sect the anonymous Praedestinatus mentions. They claimed a Christian ought to hide from other men while taking nourishment. They imagined that by eating in secret they imitated the prophets, and they based their view on certain passages of scripture.

Praedestinatus counted this their only error, but Philastrius hints they also rejected the Holy Ghost's divinity. They seem to have flourished late in the fourth century. The entry cites Hort in the Dictionary of Christian Biography, and its short record leaves the secret eaters as a small fourth-century curiosity.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-alogi:
The Alogi, from Greek a privative and logos, word, were the Deniers of the Word. Irenaeus mentions persons who denied the Paraclete's manifestation and refused the Gospel of St. John, where it is announced. He names no party. Hippolytus combated the error in his Syntagma and a work defending John and the Apocalypse. Both works are lost, though Epiphanius preserves much of them, punning alogi, without reason.

The Alogi arose in Asia Minor late in the second century, protesting Montanist abuse of the promised Paraclete, visions, and prophecies. Hence they denied the Gospel of St. John, which foretold the Holy Spirit. They refused the Apocalypse, whose Heavenly Jerusalem and thousand-year reign fed Phrygian enthusiasts. They gave both books to Cerinthus. Epiphanius is perplexed: Cerinthus made Christ mere man while John preaches his Godhead. Epiphanius implies they believed as Catholics do.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-antoine-pagi:
Antoine Pagi, a French church historian born in 1624, spent his spare years correcting Baronius. After study with the Jesuits at Aix, he joined the Conventual Franciscans at Arles and served four terms as provincial. Reading the great Annals of Baronius, he found dates and facts wrong, and made their correction his life work.

His Critica, a historical and chronological critique of the Annals, appeared in four volumes, the last three finished just before his death in 1699. His nephew edited the whole, and later editors folded it into Baronius itself. Though not free of errors, the work showed unusual care and learning, and it remains Pagi's claim to fame.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-caravaggio-mi:
Caravaggio was a Milanese painter born at Caravaggio in 1569 who died at Porto d'Ercole in 1609. Morigi was his family name, but he took his birthplace as his name and was known by it usually. The son of a mason, he mixed plaster for Milanese fresco painters as a boy and caught from them a longing to paint. He learned by copying natural objects with accuracy, a habit he rarely shook off.

After study at Venice under Giorgione's influence, he worked in Rome for Cesare d'Arpino on flowers and ornament before winning fame for his pictures. A hot temper led him to kill a friend in anger. Flight took him to Naples and Malta, where he painted the Grand Master twice and landed in prison after a quarrel. His pictures are known for startling contrasts of light and shadow and for half-length figures that seem to stand in high relief.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-francois-pagi:
Francois Pagi, nephew of Antoine Pagi, was born at Lambesc in Provence on 7 September 1654 and died at Orange on 21 January 1721, a French ecclesiastical historian. After studying with the Oratorians at Toulon he became a Conventual Franciscan, served three times as provincial, and helped his uncle correct Baronius's Annals, the great chronological history of the Church. Besides editing his uncle's Critica, he wrote his own history of the popes to 1447.

That Breviarium historico-chronologico-criticum, covering the notable deeds of Roman pontiffs and acts of general councils, appeared in four volumes at Antwerp between 1717 and 1727. His nephew Antoine Pagi the Younger continued it in two more volumes in 1748 to 1753. The entry is short because Pagi's work is a tool of scholarship rather than a life of adventure. Yet for students of papal history his critical chronology, correcting Baronius with documents and dates, remains a standard reference of its age.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-magi:
Magi were eastern sages who travelled to worship Jesus at Bethlehem. Matthew chapter 2 tells their story. This long entry asks two questions. Who were these visitors, and when did they come? It weighs evidence outside the Bible, inside it, and in early Church writers.

No Father of the Church calls them kings. The Gospel gives no number for them. Their names rest on shaky tradition alone. Persia is their likely home, a journey of 1,000 to 1,200 miles to Jerusalem. Comet theories fail to explain their star, which moved and stopped over one place. Warned in a dream, they went home by another road. They did not report back to Herod.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-salvator-tong:
Salvator Tongiorgi, philosopher, was born at Rome on 25 December 1820 and died there on 12 November 1865, just short of forty-five. Entering the Society of Jesus at seventeen, he taught rhetoric at Reggio and humanities at Forlì, then studied theology for four years under Perrone, Passaglia, Ballerini, and Patrizi. His entry in the 1913 Catholic Encyclopedia follows a short, busy teaching life.

In 1853 he took the philosophy chair at the Roman College, where for twelve years he shone as teacher and author. His Institutiones philosophicae, published in three volumes at Rome in 1861 and Brussels in 1862, ran to nine editions in eighteen years, some revised by Claude Ramière, with a compendium besides. Named assistant to the Roman provincial days before his forty-fourth birthday, his health broke within the year.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-ven-anna-mari:
Anna Maria Taigi, maiden name Giannetti, was a Venerable Servant of God, born at Siena on 29 May 1769, who died at Rome on 9 June 1837. Her parents, Luigi Giannetti and Maria Masi, ran an apothecary shop in Siena, lost everything, and moved to Rome to seek work. Anna Maria was then five years old. Schooled in domestic virtues, she married on 7 January 1789 Dominico Taigi, a retainer of the noble Chigi family, and lived happily with him for forty-eight years.

Nothing extraordinary had marked her life until one day, kneeling with her husband at the Confessio in St Peter's. There she felt a strong call to give up the small worldly vanities she had allowed herself. She began to dress plainly and heed an inner voice, taking up a life of prayer and penance amid household cares. The entry follows her gifts, her counsels, and her fame for holiness in Rome.
citizen-bird-scenes-from-bird-life-in-pl:
Citizen Bird: Scenes from Bird-Life in Plain English for Beginners, by Mabel Osgood Wright and Elliott Coues, was published in 1897 with one hundred and eleven illustrations by Louis Agassiz Fuertes. It is dedicated to all boys and girls who love birds and wish to protect them. The scene is the Orchard Farm, from spring to autumn.

A naturalist, Dr. Roy Hunter, teaches his daughter Olive and his nephew and niece Nat and Dodo, with the country boy Rap in the group. Early chapters build the bird itself: its frame, its travels, and its nest. The rest proceeds family by family, from the silver-tongued thrushes through warblers, swallows, and more.
doe-osti-3002205-in-cell-deployment-and-:
Peter Doyle, Mackenzie Ridley, Samuel Bell, Yong Yan, Jae-Kyung Han, Nathan Capps, and Jason Harp report a first inside a hot cell in Oak Ridge report ORNL/TM-2025/4113, dated September 2025. They installed digital image correlation cameras to watch an irradiated fuel rod deform during a simulated loss-of-coolant accident. The method tracks a surface pattern frame by frame to map strain, the stretching of the cladding.

Cameras recorded four frames per second during the heating test. The rod burst about 50 millimeters above the furnace center, outside the clearest camera view. The captured region showed smooth, low, uniform strain instead. Two-dimensional and three-dimensional analyses agreed on that region's trends. The team plans temperature-dependent analysis and a closer comparison of the two camera methods.
doe-osti-3363707-novel-energy-efficient-:
Jamal Yagoobi of Worcester Polytechnic Institute leads this final report (award DE-EE0009125, June 2020 to May 2024). It covers energy efficient drying for the food and pulp and paper industries. The University of Illinois and Oak Ridge National Laboratory were partners. Drying eats a large share of industrial energy, and the project targeted at least a 25 percent cut.

The team combined novel dryer designs with smart sensors and physics based models. Experiments paired infrared and ultrasound with hot air drying. They measured quality as well as energy. Total color change and browning rose with air temperature, emitter temperature, and transducer power. Hue shifted toward red and yellow. The report weighs those trade-offs for industrial adopters.
podcast-dannyjones-Jw8PQgLrLgI:
A Harvard scientist joins Danny Jones to argue that Google is running what he calls MK-Ultra 2.0: a modern mind control operation built from search rankings, recommendations, and information control rather than the drugs and torture of the CIA's original program. The episode extends the MK-Ultra story into the platform age.

The guest lays out the mechanisms as he sees them: subtle, scaled, and deniable in a way the old program never was. Jones asks how anyone could prove influence designed to be invisible. The claim is the guest's thesis, not an established finding, and Google would dispute every word of it. The recording preserves the argument because it captures a live cultural suspicion in a credentialed voice: that the feed is the experiment, and everyone reading it is a subject.
podcast-joerogan-7s_XJ5fonGI:
Roastmaster Jeff Ross joins Joe Rogan for episode 2472. Ross built fame roasting stars at Friars Club events and on TV. No insult comic works a room quite like him.

Rogan and Ross trade tales of roasts gone right and wrong. Ross shares how he writes jokes that sting but land warm. They honor dead legends of the form. The episode is brutal and fond at once. Comedy fans get a king of the roast explaining his craft, with love for the targets he burns. A roast, for him, is a love letter.
vikram-and-the-vampire-classic-hindu-tal: Sir Richard F. Burton rendered Vikram and the Vampire, classic Hindu tales of adventure, magic, and romance. His wife Isabel Burton edited the book. Pages present here hold the title page and a listing of the contents, so the tales themselves are not shown. The frame promises a preface to the first edition of 1870 and an introduction. Eleven stories told by the vampire follow. Each carries a puzzle in its title. One tells of a thief who laughed and wept. Another sets three men disputing about a woman.
